The model favors slow patterns. That means long range structure passes more strongly than rapid wiggles. We inject a faint sine wave after the early stage and track how later heads respond. The sealed sweep returned T for C1. Response rose steadily with period, and the shortest drive kept only about 35 percent [F8] of the peak gain. This pattern held across book sets.

No built-in knob could flatten the tilt. That means the bias resists simple inference settings. Scaling global and local layers returned K0 for C2. Boosting selected heads returned K0 for C3. Changing window size and rotary base both returned D0 for C4, and shuffled text kept the tilt with outcome A for C4. Shifts were small and inconsistent.

A trained adapter can dial the tilt down, but it missed its goal. That means control is possible yet limited. The sealed training test returned L0 for C5. At full strength the tilt change was -24 percent [F92], just short of the preregistered bar. General text quality stayed close, with worst perplexity ratio 1.008 [F97]. The sealed behavior test returned B0 for C6, with topic switch loss rising only 2 percent [F104].

The dial acts locally. That means a small early circuit carries the effect. The sealed localization returned M1 for C7. The early query key value block alone supplied 80 percent [F113] of the full tilt change. Its effect on its own heads was -73 percent [F121]. Other modules contributed little.

Exploratory maps point to diverse heads. That means some heads listen far while most listen near. This part is exploratory. Median listening range was 32 [F131] tokens, while the upper end reached 614 [F132] tokens. Short range heads mattered more for loss in exploratory mutes. What remains open is whether a stronger dial can flatten the tilt without harm and how far range behavior truly shifts.
